title-group.article-title: Efficacy of finerenone in reducing heart failure outcomes in patients with history of heart failure: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials

def.p: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction

body.p: Finerenone, a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, has been shown to lower kidney disease progression and clinical cardiovascular outcomes among patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) and type 2 diabetes mellitus [1], [2]. However, the efficacy of finerenone in reducing heart failure outcomes among patients with a history of heart failure has not been well established. Hence, we aimed to conduct a study-level meta-analysis of available phase III randomized clinical trials.

This meta-analysis was conducted and reported following the PRISMA (Preferred reporting items for systematic review and Meta-analysis) 2020 guidelines and performed according to established methods, as described previously [3]. A comprehensive systematic literature search was conducted in Pubmed and Clinicaltrials.gov utilizing predefined MeSH terms coupled with Boolean operators 'AND' and 'OR'. The search strategy included: “Finerenone”, “CKD”, “type 2 diabetes”, “heart failure”, HFpEF, HFrEF, “randomized controlled trials”. Our meta-analysis aimed to include all the multicentric, double-blind, randomized controlled trials published till July 2024 that compare the effects of finerenone with placebo on patients with a history of heart failure at baseline. Baseline continuous variables were summarized in mean (standard deviation), whereas dichotomous variables were described in frequency or percentage. We performed a conventional meta-analysis for outcomes included and adopted the DerSimonian and Laird random-effects model for the study variations. Outcomes were reported as the pooled odds ratio (OR) and their corresponding 95 % confidence interval (95 % CI). Statistical significance was met if the 95 % CI did not cross the numeric “1” and the two-tailed p-value was less than 0.05. All the analyses were conducted using STATA version 17.1 (StataCorp, College Station, Texas). In this meta-analysis, we included 2 randomized controlled trials that have been conducted in patients with CKD, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and a history of heart failure at baseline, comparing finerenone with placebo.

A total of 1,007 patients (485 patients in Finerenone and 522 patients in the placebo group) were included in the analysis. The mean age of patients was 65.95 ± 0.71 years, with 62 % male patients. 93 % of patients were having hypertension, and the mean follow-up duration was 3 years.

Pooled analysis showed that Finerenone significantly reduced the risk of first hospitalization for heart failure by 32 % (OR, 0.68 (95 %CI: 0.47–0.98), P = 0.04), I2 = 0 %) when compared with placebo. However, the risk of cardiovascular composite outcomes shows non-significant reduction (OR, 0.79 (95 %CI: 0.60–1.04), P = 1.10), I2 = 0.0 %). In contrast, finerenone-treated patients had a higher risk of hyperkalemia (OR, 2.16(95 %CI: 1.38–3.38), P < 0.001, I2 = 0 %) compared to placebo. (Fig. 1).Fig. 1
Forest plot of meta-analysis of A) First heart failure hospitalization, B) Cardiovascular composite outcomes, C) Hyperkalemia.

Our meta-analysis demonstrated that finerenone resulted in a 32 % reduction in the risk of initial hospitalization for heart failure. However, non-significant reductions were observed between the finerenone and placebo groups regarding the risk of cardiovascular composite outcomes. Notably, finerenone was associated with a significantly higher risk of hyperkalemia compared to placebo.

Preclinical studies have indicated that mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) improve left ventricular (LV) diastolic function and attenuate LV hypertrophy and myocardial fibrosis [2]. Numerous clinical investigations have evaluated the efficacy and safety of MRAs in patients with various conditions related to LV diastolic dysfunction, both with and without heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). A meta-analysis encompassing 11 randomized trials demonstrated that MRA therapy enhanced diastolic function, as assessed by echocardiography, and reduced circulating biomarkers of fibrosis, although no significant changes were observed in LV dimensions or mass [1]. According to available evidence, in addition to reducing hospitalization for heart failure, finerenone lowers the risk of composite outcomes, such as cardiovascular death or first hospitalization for heart failure by 18 % (HR: 0.82) and all-cause mortality by 9 % (HR: 0.91) compared to placebo [2]. These findings highlight its broader role in improving survival rates among high-risk patients with overlapping conditions like chronic kidney disease and type 2 diabetes. These findings underscore the therapeutic potential of finerenone in heart failure management. Moreover, the study indicated that finerenone use was not associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes. However, consistent with its pharmacological class as an MRA, finerenone was linked to a significant increase in hyperkalemia incidence, though this risk appears to be lower than that observed with spironolactone [2]. Additionally, finerenone has been shown to have a higher selectivity for the mineralocorticoid receptor compared to eplerenone, which may confer advantages in terms of cardiorenal protection, particularly in patients with comorbid conditions like chronic kidney disease (CKD) and diabetes mellitus [1]. Finerenone is also seen to be responsible for more than 30 % decrease in NT-proBNP levels in compared to eplerenone [4]. Our meta-analysis has several limitations. First, we relied on reported data rather than individual patient data, which may have affected bias in assessment due to the aggregated nature of published information. Second, the subgroup analyses of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) included relatively small heart failure patient populations. This limited sample size may reduce statistical power and generalizability, potentially affecting the external validity of the findings. These factors should be considered when interpreting the results, as they may influence the robustness and applicability of our conclusions across broader clinical contexts. In conclusion, our meta-analysis highlights the therapeutic potential of finerenone in reducing the risk of initial hospitalization for heart failure, with no significant impact on cardiovascular composite outcomes. However, finerenone is associated with an increased risk of hyperkalemia.
